title: What Is an Algorithm?
oneLiner: A finite, unambiguous sequence of steps that turns an input into an output -- independent of any programming language.
keyTakeaway: An algorithm is the PLAN; code is just one way to write that plan down in a language a computer happens to run. The same algorithm can become correct C#, correct Python, or plain numbered English steps on a napkin -- which is exactly why every lesson in this app shows the same problem solved in more than one language: the steps are the same, only the notation changes.
explanation: An algorithm is a finite, unambiguous sequence of steps that takes an input and produces an output. Every real algorithm has the same handful of properties, and it's worth naming them once instead of leaving them implicit: it takes zero or more INPUTS and produces at least one OUTPUT; every step is DEFINITE -- precise enough that there's no ambiguity about what to do next ("add the numbers" is definite; "handle it appropriately" is not); the whole thing is FINITE -- it has to actually stop after a limited number of steps, not run forever (this is the exact thing a missing base case violates in Recursion: Factorial); and each individual step is EFFECTIVE -- basic enough to actually be carried out, not another vague algorithm in disguise. Notice none of that mentions a programming language. "Find the largest of three numbers" is a complete algorithm as a numbered list on paper, before a single line of C# or Python gets written -- that language-independent description is called PSEUDOCODE, and it's usually the fastest way to plan an algorithm before fighting a specific language's syntax. Try it below: edit the three numbers and step through the plain-English algorithm, then look at the same exact logic written as real code underneath -- same steps, same order, same decisions, just a different notation for writing them down.
